subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder versus bipolar with psychotic features
stem:
You are the consultation psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27 year old man admitted 3 weeks ago with a manic episode. He was elated, had grandiose delusions of being chosen to save Australia from a foreign attack, and had not slept for 5 days. His mania has now settled with olanzapine 20 mg orally at night and sodium valproate 1000 mg twice daily. He is no longer elated.

However he continues to describe hearing voices commenting on his actions during the day and has ongoing paranoid beliefs that neighbours are watching him through his television, even when his mood is now euthymic. His mother and sister have schizophrenia. He has had three similar admissions over the last 4 years, each with mania followed by 4 to 6 weeks of persistent psychotic symptoms in the absence of mood elevation.

Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. His urine drug screen has been negative on repeat testing.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78/min; BP 122/76 mmHg; RR 14/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic mood; ongoing second person auditory hallucinations; persistent paranoid delusions
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative on repeat testing
data_table.History: Prior manias; each followed by 4 to 6 weeks of psychosis in the absence of mood elevation; family history of schizophrenia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features with treatment resistant psychosis needing antipsychotic maintenance with treatment resistant psychosis needing lifelong antipsychotic maintenance
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires the psychotic symptoms to occur only during mood episodes; in this man psychosis persists for 4 to 6 weeks after mood normalisation, which excludes this diagnosis (Source: DSM 5 TR; RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

options.text: Schizophrenia with comorbid mood episodes secondary to distress from the illness secondary to distress from the illness and its social consequences with poor prognosis for full functional recovery
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires the mood episodes to be brief relative to the total illness duration; here the mood episodes are prominent and recurrent, and the diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder better captures the pattern (Source: DSM 5 TR).

options.text: Substance induced psychotic disorder with a manic switch on olanzapine with a manic switch precipitated by starting olanzapine treatment with poor prognosis for full functional recovery over time
options.rationale: Substance induced psychotic disorder requires temporal association with substance use; repeat urine drug screens have been negative and olanzapine is not associated with a manic switch (Source: DSM 5 TR).

options.text: Delusional disorder, grandiose type with secondary depressive symptoms from ongoing social isolation rather than a primary psychotic disorder needing antipsychotic maintenance
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires the delusion to occur in the absence of prominent hallucinations, thought disorder or mood episodes; he has all three, which excludes this diagnosis (Source: DSM 5 TR).

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type with prominent recurrent mood episodes across the illness course and requiring combination of antipsychotic maintenance with a mood stabiliser as long term treatment
options.rationale: Schizoaffective disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms persist for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode across the illness course and mood episodes are present for the majority of the total illness; his 4 to 6 week periods of psychosis without mood elevation across multiple admissions fits this criterion (Source: DSM 5 TR; RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms persist for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode across the total illness course, and mood episodes are present for the majority of the total illness. It is distinguished from bipolar I with psychotic features by the persistence of psychotic symptoms outside mood episodes, and from schizophrenia by the prominence of recurrent mood episodes. Family history of schizophrenia is more common in schizoaffective than in bipolar disorder. Management combines a mood stabiliser with an antipsychotic; clozapine is considered when there is treatment resistant psychosis or persistent suicidality.
key_points: Schizoaffective needs at least 2 weeks of psychosis without a mood episode.
Mood episodes must be present for the majority of the illness course.
Bipolar I with psychotic features: psychosis only during mood episodes.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about persistent psychosis outside mood episodes when reviewing a patient with recurrent mania; if it persists for 2 weeks or more the diagnosis shifts from bipolar I with psychotic features to schizoaffective disorder, which changes long term prognosis and medication selection.

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar in the emergency department. A 38 year old man is brought in by his flatmate with acute confusion and shaking that started 8 hours ago. He was recently started on sertraline 100 mg orally daily 3 weeks ago and had an additional tramadol 100 mg orally 12 hours ago for a musculoskeletal back pain. He has not started or increased any antipsychotic.

On examination he is diaphoretic, agitated, and has bilateral lower limb clonus with hyperreflexia. His pupils are 6 mm and reactive. Muscle tone is normal in the arms and increased in the legs.

Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 158/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C. Bloods show creatine kinase 480 U/L (30-250), sodium 138 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, glucose 6.8 mmol/L. ECG sinus tachycardia. Point of care urine drug screen negative.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min; BP 158/98 mmHg; RR 24/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 38.9 C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic; agitated; bilateral lower limb clonus; hyperreflexia; pupils 6 mm reactive; tone normal in arms, increased in legs
data_table.Investigations: CK 480 U/L (30-250); Na 138 mmol/L; creatinine 88 micromol/L; glucose 6.8 mmol/L; ECG sinus tachycardia; UDS negative
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg for 3 weeks; tramadol 100 mg 12 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Serotonin syndrome triggered by the interaction between sertraline and tramadol and requiring cessation of the serotonergic drugs, benzodiazepines and active cooling
options.rationale: The rapid onset within 24 hours of adding a second serotonergic drug, lower limb predominant clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, agitation, diaphoresis and hyperthermia fit the Hunter serotonin toxicity criteria; sertraline plus tramadol is a classic combination (Source: Hunter serotonin toxicity criteria; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome from cross reactivity between sertraline and dopamine receptors and requiring supportive care with bromocriptine and dantrolene
options.rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days to 2 weeks after an antipsychotic dose change and presents with lead pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia and stupor rather than clonus and hyperreflexia; sertraline is not a dopamine antagonist (Source: TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Malignant hyperthermia due to genetic ryanodine receptor sensitivity and requiring immediate dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg intravenous infusion
options.rationale: Malignant hyperthermia occurs after exposure to volatile anaesthetics or depolarising muscle relaxants such as suxamethonium; there is no such exposure here (Source: TG Toxicology).

options.text: Anticholinergic toxidrome from tramadol overdose and requiring supportive care with intravenous fluid and cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Anticholinergic toxidrome presents with dry hot flushed skin, mydriasis, urinary retention and delirium; the diaphoresis and hyperreflexia are inconsistent, and tramadol is primarily a serotonergic and opioid drug rather than anticholinergic (Source: TG Toxicology).

options.text: Central pontine myelinolysis from acute correction of hyponatraemia and requiring supportive care with speech and language therapy input
options.rationale: Sodium is 138 mmol/L and there has been no correction of hyponatraemia; the picture is inconsistent with central pontine myelinolysis, which presents with locked in syndrome and dysarthria (Source: TG Nephrology).

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is diagnosed using the Hunter criteria: exposure to a serotonergic drug plus spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or tremor and hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with temperature above 38 degrees Celsius and either ocular or inducible clonus. It develops within 6 to 24 hours of a new serotonergic drug or dose increase, with lower limb predominant clonus and hyperreflexia. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days to 2 weeks after an antipsychotic dose change and presents with lead pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia and mental slowing. Treatment of serotonin toxicity involves cessation of the offending drug, benzodiazepines for agitation and clonus, active cooling and cyproheptadine in severe cases.
key_points: Serotonin syndrome: lower limb clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, mydriasis; rapid onset.
NMS: lead pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, mental slowing; onset over days.
Sertraline plus tramadol is a classic serotonin syndrome combination.
explanation.pearls: Any patient on a serotonergic drug who develops lower limb clonus and hyperreflexia within 24 hours of adding tramadol should be treated as serotonin toxicity; withhold serotonergic drugs, give benzodiazepines and add cyproheptadine 12 mg orally then 2 mg every 2 hours if severe.

stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 68 year old man is brought in by ambulance with 12 hours of fever, cough with rusty sputum and confusion. His temperature at triage is 39.4 degrees C. He has a background of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and type 2 diabetes on metformin.

On examination he is drowsy but rousable and confused about the date. He has right basal crackles and dullness to percussion. Peripheries are warm with capillary refill 3 seconds.

Pulse rate 122/min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg after a 500 mL fluid bolus, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 92% on 4 L per minute via nasal prong, temperature 39.4 degrees C. Lactate 3.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). Blood cultures have been drawn and a portable chest radiograph shows a right lower lobe consolidation. His weight is 82 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122/min; BP 88/54 mmHg after 500 mL bolus; RR 28/min; SpO2 92% on 4 L/min nasal prong; T 39.4 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy; confused about the date; right basal crackles; dull to percussion; capillary refill 3 sec; warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 3.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); CXR: right lower lobe consolidation; blood cultures drawn

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step within the hour one bundle?

options.text: Give intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g and azithromycin 500 mg orally, and reassess response after 2 hours
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone at 1 g is under dosed for severe community acquired pneumonia and oral azithromycin is inappropriate in a septic drowsy patient; the correct regimen for severe pneumonia with septic shock is broader with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus intravenous azithromycin or intravenous ceftriaxone at higher dose plus intravenous azithromycin (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Give intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg within the hour, plus further fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: In septic shock the Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour one bundle requires antibiotics within one hour together with 30 mL/kg crystalloid; the eTG antibiotic guideline for severe community acquired pneumonia is intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Commence noradrenaline peripherally at 5 micrograms per minute before further fluid resuscitation is complete
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation to 30 mL/kg is completed first while vasopressors are prepared; starting noradrenaline without adequate fluid loading is not first line unless there is contraindication to further fluids (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

options.text: Perform urgent computed tomography scan of the chest to characterise the consolidation before starting antibiotics
options.rationale: Antibiotics are not delayed for imaging in septic shock; a portable chest radiograph is sufficient to guide first line antimicrobial therapy and further imaging can follow after resuscitation (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

options.text: Give intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g monotherapy and add atypical cover only if the patient deteriorates
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin monotherapy does not cover atypical pathogens or resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae; severe pneumonia in Australia requires both third generation cephalosporin cover and atypical cover concurrently (Source: TG Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: In septic shock the Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour one bundle mandates measurement of lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, 30 mL/kg intravenous crystalloid, broad spectrum antibiotics within one hour, and vasopressors if the mean arterial pressure remains below 65 mmHg after fluids. For severe community acquired pneumonia the eTG antibiotic guideline recommends intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. Vasopressors are commenced after or during fluid resuscitation, not before it. Imaging beyond a portable chest radiograph is deferred until after resuscitation.
key_points: Antibiotics within 1 hour of septic shock recognition.
Severe community acquired pneumonia: ceftriaxone 2 g plus azithromycin 500 mg intravenously.
30 mL/kg crystalloid before or with vasopressors.
explanation.pearls: For severe community acquired pneumonia in Australia default to intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily; the atypical cover matters even when the radiograph looks lobar because Legionella can present with dense consolidation.

stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 42 year old woman with 24 hours of loin pain, rigors and dysuria. She is nauseated but tolerating small sips. She has no vomiting and no drug allergies. She takes no regular medications and has not been in hospital recently.

On examination she looks unwell but not septic. She has right loin tenderness on percussion. Abdomen is otherwise soft.

Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 122/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C. Urine dipstick leucocytes 3 plus, nitrites positive, blood 1 plus. She is 12 weeks post partum from a first pregnancy and is not currently breastfeeding. She has no known renal impairment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96/min; BP 122/72 mmHg; RR 18/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 38.6 C
data_table.Examination: Unwell but not septic; right loin tenderness on percussion; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick leucs 3+, nitrites positive, blood 1+
data_table.History: 12 weeks post partum; not breastfeeding; no drug allergies; no regular medications; no recent hospital

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally once daily for 3 days and outpatient review and safety netting for any worsening loin pain or systemic symptoms
options.rationale: Trimethoprim monotherapy is inadequate for pyelonephritis because tissue penetration and coverage of E coli in Australia is limited; a longer course and different agent are required (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid 875 plus 125 mg orally twice daily for 10 days and general practitioner review at 48 hours
options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid is a second line oral option; it is used when there is beta lactam allergy exclusion and local sensitivities support it, but the current eTG first line for pyelonephritis at home is oral trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole or cefalexin depending on culture (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 10 to 14 days after a urine sample is sent for culture and susceptibility
options.rationale: For non pregnant, non septic pyelonephritis that can be managed as an outpatient with reliable oral intake the eTG first line is oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 10 to 14 days with urine culture guiding subsequent choice, plus safety netting and 48 hour review (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg once and admit for further doses for further intravenous antibiotic therapy on the ward round
options.rationale: Intravenous gentamicin is used for hospitalised patients with severe pyelonephritis; this woman meets criteria for outpatient oral treatment given absence of sepsis, tolerating oral intake and no comorbidity (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6 hourly for 5 days after a urine sample is sent for further review with the general practitioner in 48 hours
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin has poor tissue penetration and is not recommended for pyelonephritis; it is reserved for uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection (Source: TG Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Pyelonephritis in a non pregnant adult who is not septic and tolerates oral intake can be managed at home with a 10 to 14 day course of oral antibiotics guided by a pre treatment urine culture. The eTG antibiotic first line oral options are trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole or cefalexin. Trimethoprim monotherapy and nitrofurantoin are inadequate because of poor tissue penetration. Admission for intravenous therapy is indicated for severe illness, pregnancy, inability to tolerate oral intake, or failure of outpatient therapy at 48 hours.
key_points: Outpatient pyelonephritis: 10 to 14 days oral, culture guided.
First line oral: trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole or cefalexin.
Admit for pregnancy, sepsis, vomiting or failure to improve at 48 hours.
explanation.pearls: Send a mid stream urine for culture before starting any antibiotic for pyelonephritis, then switch to a narrow spectrum agent once susceptibilities are known; empirical cefalexin covers most E coli in Australia while sparing higher generation agents.

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of necrotising fasciitis from cellulitis
stem:
You are the surgical registrar on call reviewing a 62 year old man with a 24 hour history of a red painful right lower leg after a scratch from a garden hedge. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. His pain has escalated over the last 6 hours and is now out of keeping with the appearance of the skin.

On examination the right calf is diffusely red, warm and tense over 20 cm of skin. There is exquisite tenderness beyond the erythematous margin and a small area of dusky discolouration. Sensation is intact but blistering is starting to form.

Pulse rate 116/min, blood pressure 102/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C. Bloods show white cell count 22.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 380 mg/L (less than 5), sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 138 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 12.4 mmol/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L. Point of care lactate 3.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). LRINEC score is calculated at 8.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 116/min; BP 102/60 mmHg; RR 22/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 38.6 C
data_table.Examination: Right calf diffusely red; warm; tense; tenderness beyond the erythematous margin; small dusky area; early blistering
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); CRP 380 mg/L (<5); Na 132 mmol/L; creatinine 138 micromol/L (60-110); glucose 12.4 mmol/L; Hb 128 g/L; lactate 3.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); LRINEC 8
data_table.History: T2DM; hypertension; scratch from garden hedge 24 h ago; escalating pain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g and observe the response overnight before further imaging
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy is inadequate for a suspected necrotising fasciitis with pain out of keeping and LRINEC score of 8; observation delays surgical source control and increases mortality (Source: TG Antibiotic; eMJA necrotising soft tissue infection).

options.text: Contrast enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the leg to confirm the diagnosis before any surgical involvement
options.rationale: Imaging must not delay operative source control in suspected necrotising fasciitis; a high LRINEC score together with the clinical picture is enough to proceed directly to theatre (Source: eMJA necrotising soft tissue infection).

options.text: Aspirate any blister fluid for microscopy and culture and reassess in 4 hours before making any treatment decision
options.rationale: Aspiration and observation delay urgent operative treatment; the intraoperative findings and cultures at debridement are the definitive investigation (Source: eMJA necrotising soft tissue infection).

options.text: Urgent surgical referral for debridement now, plus broad spectrum antibiotics including meropenem, vancomycin and clindamycin
options.rationale: The combination of pain out of proportion, dusky skin, systemic toxicity and a LRINEC score of 6 or more is a surgical emergency; the treatment is immediate debridement combined with broad spectrum antibiotics including meropenem or piperacillin tazobactam, vancomycin for methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus cover and clindamycin for toxin suppression (Source: TG Antibiotic; eMJA necrotising soft tissue infection).

options.text: Elevate the limb, mark the erythematous margin with a pen and reassess after 6 hours of intravenous fluids
options.rationale: This is a treatment of simple cellulitis, not necrotising fasciitis; deferring surgical care by 6 hours in a septic patient with a high LRINEC score is inappropriate (Source: eMJA necrotising soft tissue infection).

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency in which pain out of proportion to skin appearance, systemic toxicity, dusky discolouration, crepitus or blistering distinguish it from cellulitis. The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotising Fasciitis score integrates C reactive protein, white cell count, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose; a score of 6 or more raises suspicion and 8 or more strongly supports the diagnosis. The treatment is immediate operative debridement plus broad spectrum antibiotics with meropenem or piperacillin tazobactam, vancomycin and clindamycin for toxin suppression. Imaging should not delay surgical source control.
key_points: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin, systemic toxicity: necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise.
LRINEC at least 6 raises suspicion; 8 or more strongly supports the diagnosis.
Immediate debridement plus meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin.
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin is added to the empirical regimen for necrotising fasciitis regardless of susceptibility because it suppresses streptococcal exotoxin production and reduces mortality independent of the antibiotic sensitivity result.

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic differentiation of DKA and HHS
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 78 year old woman brought in by her son for 4 days of increasing lethargy, thirst and confusion. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide, and hypertension. She has had reduced oral intake since her chest infection started a week ago.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable, with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor. There is no Kussmaul breathing. Chest reveals right basal crackles.

Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees C. Glucose 42 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), venous pH 7.32 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-30), ketones 0.6 mmol/L (less than 0.6), sodium 152 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 180 micromol/L (60-110), calculated osmolality 348 mOsm/kg (285-295).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118/min; BP 96/58 mmHg; RR 22/min; SpO2 96% RA; T 37.8 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy; rousable; dry mucous membranes; reduced skin turgor; no Kussmaul breathing; right basal crackles
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 42 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); venous pH 7.32 (7.35-7.45); bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-30); ketones 0.6 mmol/L (<0.6); Na 152 mmol/L (135-145); K 4.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); creatinine 180 micromol/L (60-110); osmolality 348 mOsm/kg (285-295)
data_table.History: T2DM on metformin and gliclazide; hypertension; reduced intake for 1 week; chest infection

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state precipitated by pneumonia requiring careful fluid resuscitation and delayed low dose insulin infusion
options.rationale: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state is defined by hypovolaemia, glucose above 30 mmol/L, arterial or venous pH above 7.30, bicarbonate above 15 mmol/L, ketones under 3 mmol/L and effective osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg; the profile here fits and pneumonia is the classical precipitant (Source: JBDS hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state guideline; TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis precipitated by pneumonia requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation and a fixed rate insulin infusion
options.rationale: DKA requires ketones at or above 3 mmol/L, pH below 7.30 and bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L; her ketones are only 0.6 mmol/L, pH is 7.32 and bicarbonate is 20 mmol/L, so DKA is excluded (Source: TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis from SGLT2 inhibitor use requiring cessation of the SGLT2 inhibitor and dextrose plus insulin infusion
options.rationale: Euglycaemic DKA presents with glucose usually under 14 mmol/L and elevated ketones with acidosis, and requires an SGLT2 inhibitor which this woman is not taking; the profile is not consistent (Source: TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Alcohol induced ketoacidosis requiring supportive care, thiamine and dextrose infusion under monitoring with regular monitoring in a high dependency bed
options.rationale: Alcohol induced ketoacidosis presents with low or normal glucose, elevated ketones and a history of chronic alcohol use; there is no alcohol history and glucose is markedly elevated (Source: TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Lactic acidosis due to metformin accumulation in acute kidney injury requiring supportive care, cessation of metformin and possible haemodialysis
options.rationale: Metformin lactic acidosis produces a low pH with an elevated lactate; her pH is 7.32 and there is no reported lactic acidosis in the profile, and it does not explain the marked hyperglycaemia and hyperosmolality (Source: TG Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state is a hyperglycaemic emergency in older patients with type 2 diabetes precipitated by infection or intercurrent illness. It is defined by hypovolaemia, glucose above 30 mmol/L, arterial or venous pH above 7.30, bicarbonate above 15 mmol/L, ketones under 3 mmol/L, and effective serum osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg. Treatment is slower fluid replacement than DKA using 0.9% sodium chloride at 500 to 1000 mL per hour with careful sodium monitoring, and low dose insulin infusion added once glucose stops falling with fluids alone. Sudden osmotic shifts risk cerebral oedema and central pontine myelinolysis, so aim for a sodium fall of no more than 10 mmol per 24 hours.
key_points: Glucose above 30 mmol/L, osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg, ketones under 3 mmol/L.
DKA needs pH below 7.30 and ketones at or above 3 mmol/L.
Correct sodium slowly, no more than 10 mmol per 24 hours.
explanation.pearls: In hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state fluids alone will drop the glucose by 5 mmol/L per hour, so hold insulin until the fall slows below 5 mmol/L per hour to avoid rapid osmolar shifts and central pontine myelinolysis.

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice in infective endocarditis by valve type
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58 year old man with 3 weeks of fever, night sweats and weight loss. He had a mechanical mitral valve replacement 3 years ago for chronic rheumatic disease. He is on warfarin with an INR at target of 3.0. He has had no recent dental or surgical procedures.

On examination he has a splenomegaly of 3 cm below the costal margin, splinter haemorrhages on his fingers and a new pansystolic murmur at the apex.

Pulse rate 102/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C. Three sets of blood cultures have been drawn from separate venepunctures. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a 12 mm vegetation on the mitral prosthetic valve with moderate paravalvular regurgitation. Bloods show haemoglobin 108 g/L, white cell count 12.4 x10^9/L, CRP 128 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 92 micromol/L. He has no beta lactam allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102/min; BP 118/76 mmHg; RR 20/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 38.6 C
data_table.Examination: Splenomegaly 3 cm; splinter haemorrhages; new pansystolic murmur at apex
data_table.Investigations: TTE: 12 mm vegetation on mitral prosthesis with moderate paravalvular regurgitation; Hb 108 g/L; WCC 12.4 x10^9/L; CRP 128 mg/L (<5); creatinine 92 micromol/L; 3 sets of blood cultures drawn
data_table.History: Mechanical mitral valve 3 years ago; warfarin INR 3.0; no recent procedures; no beta lactam allergy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 2.4 g every 4 hours and gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours for 4 to 6 weeks with regular clinical and echocardiographic review
options.rationale: This regimen covers viridans streptococci for native valve endocarditis but does not cover Staphylococcus aureus adequately or coagulase negative staphylococci which are the dominant organisms in prosthetic valve endocarditis (Source: TG Antibiotic; ESC infective endocarditis guideline).

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin, intravenous gentamicin and intravenous rifampicin, adjusted to trough levels once available with cardiothoracic surgical review for consideration of prosthetic valve replacement
options.rationale: Prosthetic valve endocarditis requires empirical cover for methicillin resistant staphylococci and coagulase negative staphylococci; the eTG combination is vancomycin, gentamicin and rifampicin, with rifampicin added after the first 3 to 5 days for prosthetic material penetration once blood cultures are cleared (Source: TG Antibiotic; ESC infective endocarditis guideline).

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours and intravenous gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours for 4 to 6 weeks with regular clinical and echocardiographic review
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin covers only methicillin sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and misses coagulase negative staphylococci and methicillin resistant organisms that are common in prosthetic valve endocarditis (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily as monotherapy for streptococcal cover for 4 to 6 weeks with regular clinical and echocardiographic review with clinical review and repeat echocardiography
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy is used for penicillin susceptible viridans streptococcal native valve endocarditis; it is inadequate for empirical prosthetic valve cover where staphylococcal disease dominates (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous daptomycin as monotherapy for staphylococcal cover in prosthetic valve endocarditis with cardiothoracic surgical review for consideration of valve replacement
options.rationale: Daptomycin is inactivated by lung surfactant and is not used as sole empirical therapy for prosthetic valve endocarditis; combination therapy with vancomycin, gentamicin and rifampicin is standard (Source: TG Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Prosthetic valve infective endocarditis is dominated by staphylococcal disease, in particular coagulase negative staphylococci and methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and requires broader empirical cover than native valve disease. The eTG antibiotic regimen is intravenous vancomycin plus intravenous gentamicin plus intravenous rifampicin, with rifampicin often added at day 3 to 5 once blood cultures are clear because of the biofilm penetration required for prosthetic material. Native valve infective endocarditis is treated empirically with benzylpenicillin and gentamicin, or flucloxacillin and gentamicin depending on the suspected organism, and adjusted once cultures return. Surgical review is indicated for large vegetations, heart failure, uncontrolled infection or perivalvular extension.
key_points: Prosthetic valve empirical therapy: vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin.
Native valve empirical therapy: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin.
Rifampicin added at day 3 to 5 for biofilm penetration.
explanation.pearls: For prosthetic valve endocarditis rifampicin is added 3 to 5 days after other antibiotics have cleared bloodstream bacteraemia to reduce the risk of rifampicin resistance emerging in a large bacterial load.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and management of adrenal crisis on chronic steroids
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 62 year old woman brought in by her husband with 2 days of vomiting, abdominal pain and increasing weakness. She has been on prednisolone 15 mg daily for the last 4 years for polymyalgia rheumatica. She stopped her tablets 3 days ago because of the vomiting. She has no diabetes and no known cardiac history.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable. She has mild epigastric tenderness. Peripheries are cool with capillary refill 4 seconds.

Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg after 1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C. Bloods show sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), urea 10.4 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L, cortisol pending, TSH within normal limits. ECG sinus tachycardia. She has a chest infection which has been treated with amoxicillin over the last 5 days by her general practitioner.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min; BP 78/44 mmHg after 1 L saline; RR 22/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 37.4 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy; rousable; mild epigastric tenderness; capillary refill 4 sec; cool peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Na 128 mmol/L (135-145); K 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); urea 10.4 mmol/L; creatinine 128 micromol/L; cortisol pending; TSH within normal limits; ECG sinus tachycardia
data_table.Medications: Prednisolone 15 mg daily for 4 years; stopped 3 days ago; recent amoxicillin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give hydrocortisone 50 mg orally once glucose is corrected and reassess before further steroid and repeat the sodium, potassium and glucose measurements in 1 hour
options.rationale: Oral hydrocortisone is inappropriate in a vomiting hypotensive patient; parenteral hydrocortisone is required (Source: TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Wait for the cortisol result before commencing steroid replacement to avoid interfering with the diagnostic test and reassess the blood pressure and level of consciousness in 1 hour
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis treatment is not delayed for confirmatory testing; a random cortisol is drawn before steroid is given but treatment proceeds immediately (Source: TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously and continue aggressive fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride and 10 percent dextrose for hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis in a patient on chronic corticosteroid with intercurrent illness who has stopped their medication is a life threatening emergency; the immediate treatment is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg with continued 0.9% sodium chloride resuscitation and correction of hypoglycaemia with 10 percent dextrose (Source: TG Endocrinology; Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency guideline).

options.text: Give fludrocortisone 0.1 mg orally to correct the hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia and repeat the sodium, potassium and glucose measurements in 1 hour
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid used for chronic maintenance in primary adrenal insufficiency; it is not first line in acute adrenal crisis, where high dose hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity (Source: TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg to avoid interfering with cortisol assay and admit to the ward for handover to the general medical team once she is stable
options.rationale: Dexamethasone does not provide mineralocorticoid activity, which matters when hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia are present; hydrocortisone is preferred and cortisol can be drawn before administration (Source: TG Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis develops in patients on chronic corticosteroids or with primary adrenal insufficiency when an intercurrent illness increases cortisol requirements and endogenous production cannot rise. It presents with hypotension refractory to fluids, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and shock. The immediate treatment is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg, aggressive fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride, correction of hypoglycaemia and treatment of the precipitant. Any patient on the equivalent of more than 5 mg of prednisolone daily for more than 3 weeks is at risk and needs a sick day plan with double or triple dosing during acute illness.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously as first line in adrenal crisis.
Prednisolone above 5 mg daily for over 3 weeks needs sick day dosing.
Draw random cortisol before steroid but never delay treatment.
explanation.pearls: Any patient on chronic corticosteroids should double their oral steroid on the first sick day and switch to intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg every 8 hours if vomiting or unable to swallow, delivered from a home sick day pack.

subtopic_detail: Screening test choice for Cushing's syndrome
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 42 year old woman with 18 months of weight gain, new hypertension, and violaceous abdominal striae. She has type 2 diabetes diagnosed 6 months ago that is difficult to control on metformin plus dapagliflozin. She takes no steroids and does not use inhaled corticosteroids. She drinks less than 4 standard drinks per week.

On examination she has central obesity, a dorsocervical fat pad, thin skin with easy bruising and proximal muscle weakness. She has striae up to 2 cm wide on her abdomen. She has 3 hospital admissions with vertebral compression fractures in the last year.

Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 158/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C. Fasting glucose 9.2 mmol/L, HbA1c 8.4 percent (less than 5.7), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), TSH within normal limits. She does not have a shift work pattern or any recent stress that would perturb her circadian rhythm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84/min; BP 158/98 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Central obesity; dorsocervical fat pad; thin skin with easy bruising; proximal muscle weakness; 2 cm violaceous abdominal striae
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 9.2 mmol/L; HbA1c 8.4% (<5.7); K 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); TSH within normal limits
data_table.History: 18 months symptoms; new T2DM 6 months on metformin plus dapagliflozin; 3 vertebral fractures in 1 year; no exogenous steroids; no shift work

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial screening test?

options.text: Random serum cortisol drawn at any time of day, with confirmatory ACTH if elevated
options.rationale: A single random cortisol is not a screening test for Cushing's syndrome; cortisol is pulsatile and stress reactive and a single value has poor sensitivity or specificity (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's syndrome guideline).

options.text: Insulin tolerance test with hypoglycaemia challenge to demonstrate cortisol response
options.rationale: The insulin tolerance test is a second line dynamic test used to assess adrenal reserve or pituitary function, not a screening test for Cushing's syndrome; it is contraindicated in patients with ischaemic heart disease or seizures (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's syndrome guideline).

options.text: Serum ACTH concentration and inferior petrosal sinus sampling to distinguish source
options.rationale: Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is a second line localisation test used to distinguish pituitary from ectopic ACTH after Cushing's syndrome is confirmed biochemically; it is not a screening test (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's syndrome guideline).

options.text: 24 hour urinary free cortisol collected on at least two occasions
options.rationale: For adult Cushing's screening the Endocrine Society recommends any one of 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two occasions, late night salivary cortisol on two nights, or the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test as first line; her stable circadian rhythm and lack of shift work make urinary free cortisol reliable and it avoids the false positives of stress activated cortisol from a single measurement (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's syndrome guideline; TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Adrenal computed tomography scan with contrast to identify a cortisol producing adenoma
options.rationale: Imaging is a localisation study performed after biochemical confirmation; imaging before biochemistry produces incidentaloma related distraction and is not first line (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's syndrome guideline).

explanation.summary: The Endocrine Society Cushing's syndrome guideline recommends one of three screening tests as first line: 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two occasions, late night salivary cortisol on two nights, or the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test. Choice depends on patient factors: shift work invalidates salivary and 24 hour urinary tests based on a standard rhythm, and adherence issues limit dexamethasone suppression. Serum ACTH, imaging and inferior petrosal sinus sampling are localisation tests performed only after biochemical confirmation. Bilateral vertebral compression fractures, hypokalaemia and difficult to control diabetes in a young adult should trigger a screening test.
key_points: First line screening: 24 hour urinary free cortisol, late night salivary cortisol or 1 mg dexamethasone suppression.
Perform at least two of the same test to reduce false positives.
Imaging is a localisation test, performed after biochemical confirmation.
explanation.pearls: A red flag combination for Cushing's is difficult to control diabetes plus new hypertension plus fragility fracture plus hypokalaemia in an adult under 50; screen with 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two occasions before any imaging.

subtopic_detail: Reversal of dabigatran in life threatening bleeding
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department. A 78 year old man is brought in by ambulance after a witnessed collapse followed by right sided weakness. He takes dabigatran 150 mg orally twice daily for non valvular atrial fibrillation; last dose was 6 hours ago. He also takes ramipril and atorvastatin. He has no other bleeding history and no known renal impairment.

On examination he has a dense right hemiparesis, aphasia and left sided gaze deviation. NIHSS is 22.

Pulse rate 92/min irregular, blood pressure 168/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C. Non contrast computed tomography of the brain shows a 45 mL left temporo parietal intraparenchymal haemorrhage with intraventricular extension and 4 mm midline shift. Bloods show haemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 234 x10^9/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), INR 1.4, aPTT 42 seconds (25-35), point of care dilute thrombin time is prolonged.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92/min irregular; BP 168/94 mmHg; RR 18/min; SpO2 96% RA; T 36.7 C; NIHSS 22
data_table.Examination: Dense right hemiparesis; aphasia; left gaze deviation
data_table.Investigations: CT brain: 45 mL left temporo parietal intracerebral haemorrhage with intraventricular extension and 4 mm midline shift; Hb 128 g/L; platelets 234 x10^9/L; creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110); INR 1.4; aPTT 42 sec (25-35); dilute thrombin time prolonged
data_table.Medications: Dabigatran 150 mg BD, last dose 6 h ago; ramipril; atorvastatin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal strategy?

options.text: Give 4 factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 units/kg intravenously as a single infusion and admit to a monitored bed with hourly neurological observations
options.rationale: 4 factor prothrombin complex concentrate is the reversal for factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban when andexanet is unavailable and is used off label for warfarin bleeding; it is not the first line reversal for dabigatran because a specific antibody exists (Source: TG Haematology).

options.text: Give vitamin K 10 mg intravenously and fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg and admit to a monitored bed with hourly neurological observations for the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma reverse warfarin; they do not reverse dabigatran, which is a direct thrombin inhibitor unaffected by clotting factor replacement (Source: TG Haematology).

options.text: Give tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously and platelet transfusion and admit to a monitored bed with hourly neurological observations
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid may be adjunctive but does not reverse dabigatran; platelets do not restore thrombin activity blocked by a direct thrombin inhibitor (Source: TG Haematology).

options.text: Perform urgent haemodialysis to remove dabigatran without giving pharmacological reversal while admitting to a monitored bed with hourly neurological observations
options.rationale: Haemodialysis can remove dabigatran but is used as an adjunct or when idarucizumab is unavailable; when specific reversal is available it is preferred because dialysis is slower and less complete (Source: TG Haematology).

options.text: Give idarucizumab 5 g intravenously as two consecutive 2.5 g boluses and admit to a monitored bed with hourly neurological observations for the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor and idarucizumab is its specific monoclonal antibody reversal agent; it is given as two 2.5 g intravenous doses less than 15 minutes apart, and it fully reverses the anticoagulant effect within minutes in patients with life threatening bleeding (Source: TG Haematology; Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC reversal 2020).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC reversal 2020

explanation.summary: Direct oral anticoagulants require agent specific reversal in life threatening bleeding. Dabigatran is reversed with idarucizumab 5 g intravenously given as two 2.5 g doses less than 15 minutes apart; factor Xa inhibitors are reversed with andexanet alfa where available, or 4 factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 units/kg where andexanet is unavailable or unaffordable. Warfarin is reversed with intravenous vitamin K plus 4 factor prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma, guided by INR. Haemodialysis can remove dabigatran but is slower and less effective than idarucizumab, so it is used only as an adjunct or when idarucizumab is not available.
key_points: Dabigatran reversal: idarucizumab 5 g intravenously in two doses.
Factor Xa inhibitor reversal: andexanet alfa or 4 factor prothrombin complex concentrate.
Warfarin reversal: intravenous vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate.
explanation.pearls: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran within minutes and is stocked in Australian emergency departments; two consecutive 2.5 g intravenous doses less than 15 minutes apart give complete reversal for life threatening bleeding.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC reversal 2020
